title: Ashtpadi 4, salok: O virtueless one
hookLine: O ignorant and virtueless one, always remember the Lord who made you (Sukhmani 4)

lines: THE FRIEND WHO TELLS THE TRUTH.
AN ADDRESS NO ONE WOULD CHOOSE.
cards: A lot of self-help begins by telling you how great you are. You're enough. You've got this.
There's a place for that. But there's another kind of honesty some people find more freeing: the friend who says, gently, you got this one wrong. The doctor who tells you the real number.

The fourth ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens with that kind of honesty. Its first words aren't a compliment; they're an address almost no one would choose for themselves. And then, two lines later, a way home.

teach.b: Here's the salok, in paraphrase: O you without virtue, O ignorant one, keep that God always in your mind. Keep in your awareness the One who made you; Nanak, only that One will stand by you to the end.
The opening word, nirguniaar, means one with no virtues, nothing good of one's own to show. Iaaniaa means childish, ignorant, someone who doesn't yet understand. Hard words.
But listen to who they're addressed to. Not some other, worse person. Guru Arjan speaks to the listener, and in Gurbani the Gurus speak this way to their own minds as often as to anyone.
Sikhs hear it as the Guru speaking to every human being, himself included. And the salok isn't scolding for its own sake. Look at what it asks: remember.
Not first become virtuous, then you may remember God. The other way round. You with nothing to show, remember the One who made you.
The virtue comes from the remembering.

teach.h: NIBHEE NAAL: THE ONE STANDS BY YOU.
teach.b: Then the promise: nibhee naal, the One will stand by you, keep faith with you all the way. People leave; a body fails; the salok says the Maker doesn't. One more thing about the word.
Gun means quality or virtue, and Gurbani uses nirgun in two directions. Of a person, it can mean without virtue, as here. Of God, it means beyond all qualities, beyond anything that can be described.
Same root, two very different meanings, and this salok uses only the first.

how: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this salok at the start of the fourth ashtpadi; its humble address to the self is a familiar note in Gurbani, where the Gurus often speak to their own minds.

o: without qualities: of a person, without virtue
a prayer said with no words at all
a beggar with nothing left to offer anyone

games.q: you feel you have nothing good to show today. what does the fourth salok ask of you?
o: fix yourself first, then remember God.
keep in mind the One who made you, now.
games.why: the salok speaks straight to the one without virtue: keep in mind the One who made you, who alone will stand by you.

practice: Let yourself be exactly as you are today, with no achievements or good deeds to point to, just a person breathing.
If you pray, bring to mind the One who made you and say Waheguru once; if not, think of all that had to happen for you to exist, and hold that in wonder, empty-handed, for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Nirgun, without qualities: Sukhmani's fourth section, whose salok calls out to the one without virtue, keep in mind the One who made you, who alone stands by you to the end.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nirgun, without qualities; of a person, without virtue; of God, beyond all qualities.

carryVoice: Your line: remember who made you. Empty hands are enough to start. Four hundred fifty days now.
